title: Rise before the hoary head (Leviticus 19:32)
hookLine: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honor the face of the old man"
tomorrow: Saba needs knee surgery. so why is he also asking for prayers?

lines: RISE UP BEFORE THE HOARY HEAD.
cards: A crowded bus. An old man climbs on, holding the rail, and suddenly every seated person finds their phone fascinating. Nobody saw him.
Of course nobody saw him. Leviticus has a verse for that exact moment, and the strange thing is how it ends.
"Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD." Why bring God into a seat on a bus?

teach.b: Rashi, reading the Talmud, solves it. Standing up is something only your own heart can check. A person might shut their eyes, as if they never saw the old man come in, and who could prove otherwise?
So the verse adds: fear thy God. The one who knows whether you saw. That's the puzzle's first answer.

There's a second oddity: the verse names two people, the hoary head, and the old man. The Talmud, in the tractate Kiddushin, argues over who counts. One view reads the old man as someone who has gained wisdom.
Isi ben Yehuda says the hoary head means any elderly person at all, learned or not. Years alone are worth standing for.

teach.h: HOW MUCH HAS PASSED OVER THESE.
teach.b: And the Talmud tells of Rabbi Yochanan, who would rise even for elderly Arameans, people outside his own community, and say: how many experiences have passed over these. Not their status. Not their faith.
What their lives had carried. So an eighty-year-old standing for someone older isn't backwards.
Every age owes honor to the ones further down the road. Something to tell a friend tonight: a sage in the Talmud stood up for elders of another people, because of everything their years had seen.

how: Jewish law draws on Leviticus 19:32 for rising when an elderly person or a scholar enters, and the verse is often taught as the root of honoring the old.

games.q: what does “rise before the hoary head” mean?
o: advice to stay young at heart as you age
a law for priests to stand when sacrifices begin
a command to stand for the old and honor them

games.q: who's in the verse, and who argued — tap the pairs.
p: only your heart knows if you saw

s: Leviticus 19:32 ends with a reminder to fear God
and thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD. only God knows if you pretended not to see.
Rabbi Yochanan stood only for elders of his own community
he rose even for elderly Arameans: how many experiences have passed over these.
standing for elders is just old-fashioned manners, not something in the Torah
it's a verse in Leviticus: thou shalt rise up before the hoary head.

games.q: you're exhausted on a crowded train. an elderly woman gets on. nobody is looking at you. what does the end of the verse add?
o: only you know whether you saw her; that's why the verse names God.
since nobody noticed you see her, it doesn't really count.
stand only if she asks; otherwise it's not your job.
games.why: Rashi: you could shut your eyes as if you never saw. so the verse adds fear thy God, the one who knows.

practice: Stand up slowly, the way you would if someone you deeply respect had just walked into the room. While you're standing, name one elder in your life, close or not, and one thing their years have carried.
Then sit, and keep them in mind for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Rise before the hoary head: Leviticus's command to stand for the old, and to remember that God sees whether you noticed them.

orig.note: Hebrew: before the hoary head you shall rise. seivah is gray hair, old age.

carryVoice: Your line: honor the old, for everything their long years have carried. See you tomorrow, then.

sources.q: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.

sources.ref: Rashi on Leviticus 19:32 (one might shut his eyes as if he had not seen; therefore, fear thy God)
Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 32b-33a (who is a zaken; Isi ben Yehuda: any hoary head; Rabbi Yochanan rising for Aramean elders)
